lesson.text: Quick memory: which two metals make bronze? (Copper and tin.) Next came a metal that is harder to work but found almost everywhere: iron.
In Britain the Iron Age began about 800 BC and lasted until the Romans came in AD 43. Iron ore is found in many places, so iron tools became common: axes, sickles and ploughs.
Iron needs a very hot fire. A blacksmith heats it red-hot and hammers it into shape on an anvil. With iron ploughs and axes, farmers cleared more land and grew more food.

Most families lived in roundhouses. The round wall was woven sticks covered in mud and straw (wattle and daub). A tall cone of thatch sat on top, and a fire in the middle gave warmth and cooked the food.
Some villages were built on hilltops and ringed by deep ditches, high earth banks and wooden fences. These are hill forts. Maiden Castle in Dorset is one of the biggest in Europe.
Hill forts were safe places to live, store grain and trade, and they showed how strong a tribe was. Tribes had chiefs, and later some made the first coins in Britain.
Iron Age Britons wrote very little down. We learn about them from what archaeologists find, and from Roman writers, who were outsiders and did not always understand them.
Try it in the world: build an Iron Age roundhouse with a pointed roof of hay and a fire in the middle. Then build a hill fort: ditches and a fence around a hilltop village.

exercises.hint: The name has two clues: hill and fort.
choices: a village on a hilltop with ditches and banks
exercises.explain: A hill fort was a hilltop village protected by ditches, earth banks and wooden fences.

exercises.prompt: Most Iron Age families lived in roundhouses.
exercises.hint: Remember the lesson's houses with cone-shaped roofs.
exercises.explain: True: roundhouses had round walls, a thatched roof and a fire in the middle.

exercises.prompt: Who heats iron and hammers it into shape?
exercises.hint: This worker uses a hot fire and an anvil.
exercises.explain: A blacksmith heats iron red-hot and hammers it into tools on an anvil.

exercises.prompt: In Britain, the Iron Age came after the Bronze Age.
exercises.explain: True: the Stone Age, then the Bronze Age, then the Iron Age.

exercises.prompt: What was a roundhouse's roof made of?
exercises.hint: It was made from plants that farmers grew or cut.
exercises.explain: Roundhouse roofs were thatched with straw or reeds, in a tall cone shape.

exercises.prompt: Why did iron tools become more common than bronze ones?
exercises.hint: To make bronze you needed copper and tin from different places. What about iron?
choices: iron ore is found in many places
exercises.explain: Iron ore is found in many places, so iron was easier to get than copper and tin.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: The ages are named after the tools, from oldest to newest.
exercises.explain: The Stone Age, the Bronze Age, the Iron Age (from about 800 BC), then the Romans in AD 43.

exercises.prompt: Iron Age Britons wrote many books about their lives.
exercises.hint: Remember how we learn about them.
exercises.explain: False: they wrote very little, so we learn from archaeology and from Roman writers.

exercises.prompt: Why did people build hill forts on hilltops?
exercises.hint: What can you see from a hilltop, and how easy is it to climb one?
choices: to see far and be hard to attack
to be closer to the stars
exercises.explain: From a hilltop you can see who is coming, and the slopes, ditches and banks make it hard to attack.

exercises.prompt: A Roman writer describes the Iron Age Britons. Why should a detective be careful?
exercises.hint: Would a visitor from far away understand everything about you?
choices: he was an outsider who may not have understood
it is a primary source, so it must be true
exercises.explain: The writer was an outsider, so he may have got things wrong or told only his side.

exercises.prompt: With iron ploughs and axes, farmers could clear more land and grow more food.
exercises.hint: Iron tools were strong and common. What could farmers do with more of them?
exercises.explain: True: iron tools helped farmers clear forests and plough more fields.

exercises.prompt: Maiden Castle has several rings of banks and ditches. What were they for?
exercises.hint: Imagine trying to climb over bank after bank.
choices: making the fort harder to attack
exercises.explain: Each ring of banks and ditches made the hill fort harder to reach and safer to live in.

exercises.prompt: Where was the fire in a roundhouse?
exercises.hint: Where would it warm everyone best?
choices: in the middle of the floor
exercises.explain: The fire was in the middle, so everyone could sit around it; the smoke seeped out through the thatch.

exercises.prompt: Match each tool to the age it comes from.
exercises.hint: Stone tools were chipped, bronze was poured into moulds, and iron was hammered.
exercises.explain: The flint axe is from the Stone Age, the cast axe from the Bronze Age, and the hammered plough from the Iron Age.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: Iron Age or Stone Age?
exercises.hint: Which ones need metal, and which came long before metal?
exercises.explain: Iron ploughs and hill forts are Iron Age; flint axes and cave paintings of mammoths are Stone Age.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: Stone Age, Bronze Age or Iron Age?
items: an axe cast in a mould
exercises.hint: Stone tools first, then bronze cast in moulds, then iron hammered by a smith.
exercises.explain: Stone Age: flint axes and cave paintings. Bronze Age: copper and tin melted into bronze and cast in moulds. Iron Age: blacksmiths hammering on anvils, and hill forts.

exercises.prompt: The Iron Age in Britain began about 800 BC and lasted until AD 43. About how many years did it last?
exercises.hint: Count the BC years down to the start of AD, then add the AD years.
exercises.explain: BC years count down to the start of AD: about 800 years. Then 43 more years to AD 43: 800 + 43 = 843. So the Iron Age lasted over 800 years.

exercises.prompt: Order how a roundhouse was built.
items: Light a fire in the middle.
Put up a tall cone of thatch.
Weave sticks into a round wall.
Cover the wall in mud and straw.
exercises.hint: Walls before the roof, and the fire last, once the house is closed in.
exercises.explain: Weave sticks into a round wall (wattle), cover it in mud and straw (daub), put up the tall cone of thatch, then light the fire in the middle.
